title: Ang 489: Gujri begins
hookLine: Guru Nanak opens the morning raga
tomorrow: who feeds a creature that lives inside a rock?

lines: WHAT IF THE MIND WERE THE STONE?
cards: Morning routines online run to a dozen steps: the cold water, the journal, the supplements lined up on the counter. Gujri, a raga tradition sings in the early morning, opens on ang 489 with a routine too. An old one.
Sandalwood rubbed on a wet stone into paste, saffron mixed in, a mark before worship. And Guru Nanak rewrites it with one question: what if the mind were the grinding stone?

teach.h: NAME AS SANDALWOOD, MIND AS STONE.
teach.b: In paraphrase: I'd make your Name the sandalwood, if my mind were the grinding stone.

If good deeds were the saffron mixed in, worship would happen inside. Then the line that sets the rule: worship means dwelling on the Name; without the Name, there is no worship. Notice what he keeps.
Not one picture is thrown out.

teach.h: ONE READING: THE INSIDE IS THE POINT.
teach.b: The stone, the paste, the saffron all stay; they just move inside. And that's where Sikhs read this page in more than one way. Some put the weight on the inside.
Their best case is the text itself: without the Name, no ritual counts, however carefully it's done.

teach.h: ANOTHER: THE HANDS TRAIN THE HEART.
teach.b: A perfect outward form with an empty heart is paste on a forehead and nothing more. Others put the weight on the hands.
Their best case is also in the text: the Guru reached for a real, physical routine to describe the inner one.

Sikhs who keep the rehat, cover their heads before the Granth and rise early for the morning prayers often say the outward practice is exactly how the mind gets ground smooth. Both readings start from the same page.
Neither one says the inside doesn't matter. The question between them is how the stone gets turned.

how: Sikhs reading the Granth in order reach Gujri after Asa; its hymns are sung in kirtan, and Guru Nanak's opening hymn is often explained in katha as worship moved inward.

o: the page where the raga of Gujri begins
a page on how to grind sandalwood paste
the last page of the Bhagats in Asa

games.q: the inner routine — tap the pairs.

s: Guru Nanak's first Gujri hymn throws the old words of worship away
he keeps the sandalwood, the stone and the saffron, and moves them inside.
the hymn says that without the Name there is no worship
worship means dwelling on the Name; without it, none happens.
Sikhs all read this hymn to mean outward practice is pointless
readings differ: some stress the inside, others say the outward form helps train it.

games.q: your cousin says the rehat and the dress don't matter, only the heart, and points to ang 489. you see it the other way. what's the strongest case for his side?
o: the text says without the Name there's no worship, however careful the ritual.
outward things are always fake, so anyone who keeps them is pretending.
the Guru threw out sandalwood and saffron, so no outward form is allowed.
games.why: his best case is the text itself. and the Guru kept the stone and saffron as pictures, which is the other side's best case. both start from the same page.

practice: Say the Guru's picture out loud, slowly, in your own words: the Name the sandalwood, the mind the stone, good deeds the saffron. Then rest your hands open on your knees for the sit, and let the words settle.
If you'd like to read it first, it's the opening of ang 489.

wordCard.voice: Ang 489. The page where Gujri begins, with Guru Nanak moving the sandalwood, the stone and the saffron inside.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: Gujri, the raga that begins on ang 489.

carryVoice: Gujri begins with the grinding stone inside you, and the saffron in what you do. Day fifteen hundred and one, done.
